issues.legal_issue: Testimony of a related witness is not unreliable merely because of the witness’s relationship to the deceased.
material_facts: Two witnesses returning from a village gathering said they saw the accused attack the deceased in the courtyard, using the light of their torches.
The witnesses’ presence on the route was consistent with their attendance at the gathering, and their accounts were found credible, reliable, and corroborated.
Some witnesses were related to the deceased or to the person who reported the incident, but the court found no material contradictions in their testimony.
issues.conclusion: The witnesses’ testimony could be relied on; their relationships to the deceased did not, by themselves, justify rejecting it.
issues.legal_principle: Under Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, a witness is ordinarily considered independent unless there is reason to believe the witness is tainted; relationship alone is not a basis to reject testimony. State of A.P. v. S. Rayappa, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Kishanpal, and Darya Singh v. State of Punjab affirm that a related witness is not necessarily an interested witness, and credible testimony from such a witness need not invariably be corroborated. The court must assess the evidence on the facts of the case.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction and related_witnesses_testified and witnesses_had_natural_presence and testimony_was_credible and not material_contradictions

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction: The proceeding was a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.related_witnesses_testified: Witnesses who were related to the deceased or another person connected with the case gave evidence.
predicates.witnesses_had_natural_presence: The circumstances gave the witnesses a natural reason to be at the place where they observed the occurrence.
predicates.testimony_was_credible: The court found the witnesses’ accounts reliable and supported by other evidence.
predicates.material_contradictions: The witnesses’ accounts contained contradictions that materially undermined the prosecution’s case.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal challenges a conviction, related witnesses were naturally present, and their credible evidence has no material contradictions, their testimony is not rejected solely because of their relationship.

issues.legal_issue: Credible eyewitness testimony is not displaced by medical evidence unless the medical evidence rules out the occurrence in the manner described by the witnesses.
material_facts: Two eyewitnesses saw the accused restrain and attack the deceased, including with a cutting implement.
The post-mortem recorded incised wounds and neck injuries, and the doctor attributed death to asphyxia caused by strangulation.
The court found the eyewitness account and medical findings complementary and found no material inconsistency between them.
issues.conclusion: There was no material conflict between the oral and medical evidence; even an immaterial variation would not entitle the accused to benefit.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied Kapildeo Mandal v. State of Bihar, State of U.P. v. Krishan Gopal, and Bhajan Lal v. State of Haryana for the principle that oral and medical evidence should be read together and that primacy is generally given to credible oral evidence. Under Kamaljit Singh v. State of Punjab, eyewitness testimony cannot be rejected for a discrepancy unless the medical evidence completely rules out the injuries occurring as described. Madan Gopal Kakad v. Naval Dubey explains that the court evaluates expert opinion and forms its own judgment on the materials.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction and eyewitness_account_credible and medical_evidence_does_not_exclude_described_occurrence and (evidence_is_compatible or variation_is_immaterial)

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction: The proceeding was a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.eyewitness_account_credible: The court found the eyewitnesses’ account credible and trustworthy.
predicates.medical_evidence_does_not_exclude_descri: The medical evidence did not rule out the possibility that the injuries occurred in the manner described by the eyewitnesses.
predicates.evidence_is_compatible: The eyewitness account and medical findings were consistent when read together.
predicates.variation_is_immaterial: Any difference between the eyewitness account and medical findings did not materially undermine the prosecution’s case.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal, credible eyewitness evidence is not displaced when the medical evidence does not rule out the described occurrence and the evidence is compatible or differs only immaterially.

issues.legal_issue: A defect in investigation does not by itself require acquittal when the remaining prosecution evidence is reliable and the defect does not undermine the case or prejudice the accused.
material_facts: The investigating officer did not send the recovered cutting implement and blood-stained clothing for serological examination.
A witness proved the recoveries and withstood cross-examination; the recoveries were established in court.
Two eyewitnesses supported the prosecution, and two other witnesses who were present immediately after the occurrence also supported its case.
The court found the prosecution case proved beyond reasonable doubt notwithstanding the investigative lapse.
issues.conclusion: The failure to obtain a serologist’s report was a serious investigative lapse but did not give the accused an advantage or justify acquittal on the evidence in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Under Dayal Singh v. State of Uttaranchal, Sathi Prasad v. State of U.P., Dhanaj Singh v. State of Punjab, Paras Yadav v. State of Bihar, State of Karnataka v. K. Yarappa Reddy, Karnel Singh v. State of M.P., and Ram Bali v. State of U.P., the court must scrutinize the evidence independently of investigative omissions and must not acquit solely because of a defect in investigation. A defect may matter if it affects the root of the prosecution case or prejudices the accused. Zahira Habibullah Sheikh v. State of Gujarat and National Human Rights Commission v. State of Gujarat emphasize the court’s responsibility to ensure a fair trial and proper administration of justice.

rule.if: criminal_case and investigation_defect and remaining_prosecution_evidence_reliable and defect_does_not_undermine_case and not accused_prejudiced_by_defect

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding was a criminal case in which the prosecution sought to establish the accused’s guilt.
predicates.investigation_defect: The investigation omitted or mishandled a step relevant to the prosecution evidence.
predicates.remaining_prosecution_evidence_reliable: The evidence apart from the investigative defect was found reliable and sufficient to support the prosecution case.
predicates.defect_does_not_undermine_case: The investigative defect did not affect the root of the prosecution case.
predicates.accused_prejudiced_by_defect: The investigative defect caused prejudice to the accused.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, an investigative defect alone does not require acquittal when the other prosecution evidence is reliable, the defect does not undermine the case, and it has not prejudiced the accused.

issues.legal_issue: A serious investigative lapse may warrant a court-directed disciplinary inquiry against the investigating officer, including when the officer has retired.
material_facts: The investigating officer failed to obtain serological reports for recovered articles, a lapse the court described as serious.
The court directed the state police chief to take disciplinary action against the officer, whether he remained in service or had retired.

For a retired officer, the court directed that action concerning pension be taken under the applicable service rules, and that any limitation bar in those rules not prevent the inquiry directed by the court.
issues.conclusion: The police chief was directed to take disciplinary action against the investigating officer, including appropriate pension-related action if the officer had retired; a limitation bar in the applicable rules was not to prevent the court-directed inquiry.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on its assessment that the failure to obtain the serological reports was a serious investigative lapse. It also drew on the principles in Dayal Singh v. State of Uttaranchal and the authorities discussed there concerning the court’s responsibility to address defective investigation and ensure proper administration of justice. The judgment directs pension-related action in accordance with the applicable service rules.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding was a criminal case in which the court assessed the conduct of the investigation.
predicates.investigating_officer_committed_serious_: The investigating officer committed an investigative omission that the court regarded as serious.
predicates.court_directed_disciplinary_action: The court ordered the competent authority to take disciplinary action concerning the investigating officer.

issues.definition: When a court finds a serious investigative lapse in a criminal case and directs disciplinary action, action concerning the investigator’s conduct is to be taken.
